description.narrative: Girls and young women (age 14 till 24) are the primary target group of the She Leads programme. Especially those that experience intersecting forms of discrimination and exclusion such as GYW living in poor, remot rural areas and urban slums, GYW experiencing GBV, GYW with different abilities, GYW who are out of school, GYW from sexual minority groups and refugees and internally displaced GYW. In addition, the programme works closely with CSO organisations and networks, (representatives of) formal institutions and community members and leaders.

In all She Leads countries, girls and young women, particularly GYW from socially excluded and exploited groups, are denied the opportunity to voice their interests and to participate meaningfully in decision-making processes. While many countries have made impressive strides in, for example, GYW’s access to education and the introduction of new laws against GBV, their socio-political participation continues to be much lower than that of boys and young men. Within the population of girls and young women (between age 14 till 24 years of age), there are specific groups of GYW in She Leads countries who suffer most from (intersectional) discrimination and exclusion.She Leads is a joint programme of Plan International Netherlands, Defence for Children - ECPAT the Netherlands (DCI-ECPAT), African Women’s Development and Communication Network (FEMNET), and Terre des Hommes the Netherlands (TdH). Equal Measures 2030 is a technical partner. The She Leads consortium brings together child rights organisations, feminist/women’s rights organisations, and GYW-led groups and aims to increase sustained influence of girls and young women (GYW) on decision-making and the transformation of gender norms in formal and informal institutions.

The long-term aim (impact) of She Leads is that GYW’s perspectives are included in gender responsive laws and policies and societal norms and practices. The strategic objective is to increase the sustained influence of GYW on decision-making and the transformation of gender norms in formal and informal institutions.Central to the She Leads programme is the enhancement of collective action of girls and young women in a gender-responsive civil society (civil society domain), support by increased acceptance of positive social gender norms (socio-cultural domain) and by enabling meaningful participation of girls and young women in decision-making by political institutions (institutional domain).

For the past year and six months, DCI-Sierra Leone has been working with one women-led CSO.
Our partner DCI-Sierra Leone will work with the Sierra Leone Association of Women in Journalism to help expand the latter's constituencies.

Sierra Leone’s Association for Women in Journalism (SLAWIJ) was trained on the Gender, Safeguarding, Adaptive programming, and Outcome harvesting and Content gathering. Presently, the organization has developed a plan for their female journalists to gather and document changes observed related to the She Leads programme, and how its membership can promote gender issues via their different radio and television programmers. They have also acquired knowledge and the desired skills on how to gather and document signs of change relating to advocacy programme – with a tie to the She Leads Programme. The group of journalists has also acquired knowledge on safeguarding, and this has led them to develop their own safeguarding policy, and also give them the skills on how to report on gender issues and collect content. It is worthy to note that SLAWIJ has increased on their knowledge and has taken steps to design documents and plans for improvement of their programmes and initiatives focusing on girls and young women. We can safely say that this CSO has greatly improved on their capacity with more to be done when it comes to putting the knowledge into practice.

DCI-SL has been a committed partner in the She Leads consortium for Sierra Leone and has also served as an excellent coordinating organization for implementing the She Leads Programme. The team has additionally initiated several actions to enhance collaboration with the other consortium partners (Plan Sierra Leone and Women’s Forum), including working together to support GYW to produce their shadow on implementing the Maputo protocol in Sierra Leone. The organization also works with other CSOs to submit the shadow report on the same Maputo protocol. Furthermore, in 2023, DCI-SL, together with the other consortium partners, are planning to work together to engage the Political Party Registration Commission (PPRC), the Commission for National Elections and the security sector (including the police and Office of National Security) to create space for girls and young women’s participation in leadership decision-making processes as well as to develop policies and guidelines for the conduct of peaceful elections as well as the safety of girls and young women (prevention of gender-based violence) in the electioneering process.
DCI-SL will work with DCI ECPAT together to search for more opportunities to support girls and youth groups during this reporting period.

title.narrative: # of youth led CSOs with strengthened capacity to advance women's rights and gender equality

comment.narrative: Because it's the first year of implementation, the value is zero.
DCI-Sierra Leone plans to strengthen the capacity of 2 youth-led organisations on WRGE.

DCI-Sierra Leone has increased the capacity of two youth-led CSOs on Lobby, Advocacy, Safeguarding, and Project Management, using the media advocacy platform and how to collect and document signs of change related to the She Leads programme. This training has supported these groups in creating impactful online content and producing short videos and messages for social media, including WhatsApp, Instagram, Twitter, and Facebook. Most importantly, these capacity-strengthening activities have inspired 30 young people to engage in professional media trainings in videography and photography, which are now careers for three of them. However, it would be good to see that the groups design a more sustainable plan for their online advocacy and promote the priorities of the She Leads programme. In addition, based on the training received on project management, youth-led groups have improved on their capacity to design proposals and effectively implement and manage their activities and resources. However, there is a need for the group to improve on timely reporting of their programme and activities. Additionally, based on the safeguarding training acquired by the different groups, they are now taking measures to ensure the safety of the young people that are engaged in their activities in communities.
